title: A tax on gas exports would lower domestic gas prices
oneLiner: The effect claim underneath the tax proposal.
body: If exporting attracts a levy and domestic sales do not, producers have a reason to sell locally at a price below export parity, and the domestic price settles lower. Proponents argue this works through price rather than volume, so it does not depend on how much gas a reservation scheme captures or on which contracts are exempt.
contextBackground: Separated from the proposal because one can accept that a tax would lower prices and still prefer reservation, or doubt the price effect and still want the revenue.
contextDisagreement: Critics say producers with long-term export contracts would absorb or pass through the levy rather than divert gas, so the domestic price effect could be small, and that a levy set high enough to work would deter new supply.

evidenceItems.citation: ABC News, 7 May 2026 — Greens' argument that an export tax would lower domestic prices

otherClaim.title: Australia should tax gas exports rather than reserve gas for domestic buyers

claimItself.title: Australia should tax gas exports rather than reserve gas for domestic buyers
claimItself.oneLiner: The competing proposal from the Greens and Senator Pocock: price the exports, do not ration them.
claimItself.body: Instead of requiring producers to set gas aside, an export levy would make overseas sales less attractive relative to domestic ones and return revenue to the public. The Greens argued the reservation policy was written by the industry for the industry; Senator David Pocock's dissenting report to a Senate committee recommended a 25 per cent tax on all gas exports. The government ruled out gas tax increases in the May 2026 budget, citing fuel security during the Middle East conflict.
